group.passage: Lethal White, by J.K. Rowling under the name Robert Galbraith, is the fourth book in the series of Cormoran Strike books. It is set in 2012, during a time when Britain was basking in the success of the Olympics and Paralympics. Still, the novel focuses on darker and more current themes ─ corrupt officials misusing power, far-left antisemitic figures, and strained personal relationships throughout the story. With this installment, Rowling begins to display a familiar pattern. Like her Harry Potter series, her novels tend to grow huge and complex. At 647 pages, Lethal White feels bloated. The main murder doesn’t even take place until page 281. Before that, the story drifts through a large number of unrelated side plots and details. As a reader, you sense everything will eventually connect, but it takes too long to get there. Galbraith’s books are usually at their best when Strike and Robin are working closely together, balancing their complicated emotions while solving a case. Unfortunately, they spend much of this novel apart. Robin especially suffers from this distance. She often feels like a weaker version of the strong, confident woman we knew in the earlier books. Her storyline in this book paints her as naive in her marriage, and it’s hard not to believe that the Robin from the past would have already left the disappointing Matthew. However, once Strike and Robin are reunited ─ interviewing the victim’s family in a quiet Oxfordshire estate, walking together through the forest at night, and piecing together clues ─ the story finds its energy again. The charm of their partnership returns, proving that what truly engages readers is not the tension of the mystery, but the relationship between the characters. Lethal White has plenty of twists and surprises, and when its many threads finally come together, it becomes a satisfying and gripping read. Still, with better editing and a tighter pace, it could have been a truly outstanding one.
